record.paper_title: Twenty open problems in quantum control
record.original_question: Because coherent feedback implemented by unitary system-auxiliary interactions is naturally periodic rather than continuously dissipative, what forms of Hamiltonian are needed to realize continuous or quasi-continuous quantum feedback control, and in which regimes can one derive simple analytic formulas for the resulting steady-state control performance?

evidence.quote: Problem 6: Coherent feedback via unitary interactions is inherently a periodic process. What kind of Hamiltonians are required to obtain continuous or quasi-continuous control, and is it possible to obtain simple analytic expressions for steady-state performance in some regimes?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a quantum control setting in which a target quantum system, with Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}_S$, is coupled to an auxiliary quantum system ("controller"), with Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}_A$, by a joint unitary interaction $U(t) = \exp(-i H_{SA} t/\hbar)$ on $\mathcal{H}_S \otimes \mathcal{H}_A$ generated by a (possibly time-dependent) Hamiltonian $H_{SA}$. Such "coherent feedback" via unitary system–auxiliary interactions is intrinsically periodic: in the absence of dissipation or reset of the auxiliary, the joint evolution recurs and does not by itself generate a non-trivial steady state on the system alone.

Formulate and answer the following:

(a) Characterize the classes of joint Hamiltonians $H_{SA}$ (possibly augmented by repeated re-initialization, weak-coupling limits, continuous exchange of an auxiliary bath mode, or similar mechanisms) that yield genuinely continuous or quasi-continuous coherent feedback dynamics on the reduced state $\rho_S(t) = \mathrm{Tr}_A[\,U(t)(\rho_S(0)\otimes\rho_A)U(t)^\dagger\,]$, in the sense that $\rho_S(t)$ obeys an autonomous master equation (Lindblad-type or otherwise) admitting a non-trivial steady state $\rho_S^{\mathrm{ss}}$.

(b) Identify regimes — for example, weak coupling, fast re-initialization of the auxiliary, Markovian limits, or linear (Gaussian) systems — in which closed-form analytic expressions for the steady-state performance (such as fidelity to a target state, purity, entanglement, or a quadratic cost) of the resulting coherent-feedback loop can be derived, and exhibit such expressions.
artifact.status_search_result: The general question of which Hamiltonians realize quasi-continuous coherent feedback and when closed-form steady-state performance exists remains open. Partial progress exists: for linear (Gaussian) quantum systems, coherent $H^\infty$/LQG frameworks yield analytic controller designs via Lyapunov/Riccati equations, and recent work has produced closed-form steady-state covariance results under continuous monitoring with unitary feedback. However, no general theory characterizing the required Hamiltonians or yielding analytic steady-state performance beyond linear or weak-coupling regimes has been established.

status_evidence.title: Coherent feedback H^infty control of quantum linear systems
status_evidence.snippet: physically realizable quantum controllers can be obtained by solving at most four Lyapunov equations
status_evidence.claim: Analytic/closed-form coherent feedback design is available specifically for linear quantum systems via Lyapunov equations.

status_evidence.title: Open quantum systems under coherent control with continuous monitoring and unitary feedback
status_evidence.snippet: Methods have been developed to determine the control Hamiltonian that optimally counteracts a given dissipation mechanism
status_evidence.claim: Specific Hamiltonian designs for coherent feedback have been derived in restricted dissipative settings, but not as a general theory.

status_evidence.title: Quantum feedback: Theory, experiments, and applications
status_evidence.snippet: Survey of quantum feedback theory and applications
status_evidence.claim: Comprehensive review confirms continuous coherent feedback Hamiltonian design and analytic steady-state performance remain active research topics without a general resolution.
